o: Skin creases have thinner epidermis and thicker dermis

At skin creases the epidermis is thinner and the dermis thicker, and the skin is bound firmly to the underlying fascia.
That is why creases persist.
The panniculus carnosus forms palmaris brevis in man

The panniculus carnosus forms palmaris brevis in man, as well as dartos, platysma and the facial muscles.
A remnant of an animal skin muscle.
Deep fascia passes freely over bone

Last's says deep fascia is always anchored firmly to periosteum where it meets bone; it does not pass freely over it.
This compartmentalises the limbs.
Deep fascia has its own nerve supply distinct from the overlying skin

Deep fascia shares the innervation of the overlying skin; it has no separate nerve supply.
Fascial pain is localised like skin pain.
Only fibrocartilage has a blood supply

Only fibrocartilage has a blood supply; hyaline and elastic cartilage rely on diffusion.
So hyaline cartilage heals poorly.
The epiglottis is elastic cartilage

The epiglottis is elastic cartilage, as is the pinna.
Elastic cartilage does not calcify.
Secondary cartilage is the cartilage of secondary cartilaginous joints

Secondary cartilage is a special cartilage of growing membrane bones, such as the mandibular head and clavicle, not the cartilage of secondary cartilaginous joints.
The similar names are a trap.
Menisci of the knee are hyaline cartilage

The menisci of the knee are fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.
Like the intervertebral discs and TMJ disc.
Yellow ligaments include the ligamenta flava

Yellow ligaments (rich in elastic tissue) include the ligamenta flava and the capsular ligaments of the auditory ossicles.
Most ligaments are white (collagen).
The epiphyseal plate is a primary cartilaginous joint

In a primary cartilaginous joint bone meets hyaline cartilage directly, as at the epiphyseal plate; it allows no movement.
It ossifies when growth stops.
The pubic symphysis is a primary cartilaginous joint

The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), with fibrocartilage between hyaline-covered bone ends.
All symphyses are midline.
Hilton's law states that a joint's nerve supplies only its capsule

Hilton's law states that the nerve to a muscle also supplies the joint it moves and the overlying skin.
Not just the capsule.
The parietal layer of serosa develops from somatopleure

The parietal layer of a serous membrane develops from somatopleure and is supplied segmentally by spinal nerves.
So it is pain-sensitive.
The visceral layer has no sensory supply

The visceral layer has no sensory (somatic) supply, only autonomic.
So it is insensitive to cutting.
The pulmonary veins have valves

The pulmonary veins are valveless.
Like the venae cavae and portal veins.
Veins have an internal elastic lamina like arteries

Veins lack an internal elastic lamina; arteries have one.
A histological distinction.
Perineurium joins fibres into fascicles

Endoneurium surrounds each fibre, perineurium binds fibres into fascicles, and epineurium binds the fascicles into the nerve.
Perineurium is the diffusion barrier.
The phrenic nerve takes its own artery through the mediastinum

The phrenic nerve takes its own artery, the pericardiacophrenic, through the mediastinum.
An example of a nerve with a named artery.
Endoneurium binds fascicles into a nerve

Epineurium binds the fascicles into a nerve; endoneurium surrounds individual fibres.
Order from outside in: epi, peri, endo.
About 10% of fibres in a muscle nerve are afferent

About 40 percent of the fibres in a nerve to a muscle are afferent, not 10 percent.
From spindles, tendon organs and pain endings.
There are 31 pairs

There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal.
C8 has no matching vertebra.
Anterior roots contain some unmyelinated afferent pain fibres

Anterior roots contain some unmyelinated afferent pain fibres that double back from the dorsal root ganglion.
This may explain pain after posterior rhizotomy.
Spinal nerves lie in the spinal canal

The roots unite in the intervertebral foramen; no spinal nerves lie in the spinal canal.
The canal contains roots only.
The spinal nerve proper is about 1 cm long

Last's says the spinal nerve proper is only 1 to 2 mm long at best, not 1 cm.
It divides almost immediately into rami.
The trochlear and abducent nuclei are the exception to overlapping motor pools

Last's says the trochlear and abducent nuclei are the exception to overlapping motor neuron pools: each supplies a single muscle.
Other motor pools overlap.
More distal joints are controlled from lower cord segments

For each joint further down the limb, the spinal centre lies one segment lower (shoulder C5, elbow C6–7, wrist C6–7, hand C8–T1).
A Last's rule.
Cutaneous nerve lesions cause proprioceptive loss

Cutaneous nerves carry no muscle proprioceptive fibres, so their lesions do not cause proprioceptive loss.
Proprioception travels with muscle nerves.
Muscles sharing an action are usually supplied by different segments

Muscles sharing an action are usually supplied by the same segments, not different ones.
That is Last's first rule.

questions.s: Nerves and vessels of the body wall (Last's):
o: Where nerve and segmental artery cross, the nerve lies nearer the skin

Where the spinal nerve and the segmental artery cross, the nerve is always the more superficial.
A body-wall pattern.
The sympathetic trunk lies within the circle of the segmental artery

The sympathetic trunk lies vertically within the circle made by each segmental artery.
The arteries arch around the vertebral bodies.
Posterior rami supply limb muscles

Posterior rami never supply limb muscles.
Limbs are supplied by anterior rami.
The collateral intercostal branch supplies skin

The collateral branch of an intercostal nerve is motor only and does not supply skin.
It supplies the intercostal muscles.
Limb buds arise from the lateral strip of the body wall

Limb buds arise from the lateral strip of the body wall, supplied by lateral branches of the anterior rami.
Hence the limb plexuses.
Posterior divisions supply extensor compartments

Posterior divisions of the plexuses supply the extensor muscles and skin; anterior divisions supply the flexors.
A basic plan.
The extensor compartment has the richer nerve supply

The flexor compartment has the richer nerve supply; the lowest root of each plexus goes wholly to flexors.
T1 and S3.
The cephalic vein marks the postaxial border of the upper limb

The cephalic vein marks the preaxial border of the upper limb; the basilic vein marks the postaxial border.
Similarly great and small saphenous in the leg.
Brachioradialis developed in the extensor compartment

Brachioradialis developed in the extensor compartment, which is why it is supplied by the radial nerve despite flexing the elbow.
Its supply reflects origin, not action.
The adult septum imprisons the ulnar nerve in the extensor compartment above the elbow

The ulnar nerve began as a flexor-compartment nerve, but in the adult the medial intermuscular septum traps it behind, in the extensor compartment, above the elbow.
It then returns to the flexors.
The short head of biceps femoris developed in the flexor compartment

The short head of biceps femoris developed in the extensor compartment, hence its common peroneal supply.
The long head is tibial.
The radial nerve lies in the extensor compartment just above the elbow

Just above the elbow the lateral septum places the radial nerve in the flexor compartment, between brachialis and brachioradialis.
It pierced the septum to get there.
There is no dermatomal overlap across axial lines

Adjacent dermatomes overlap, but dermatomes meeting at an axial line are discontinuous and do not overlap. So sensation should be tested across axial lines.
Loss is easiest to detect there.
The upper limb anterior axial line starts near the sternal angle

The anterior axial line of the upper limb starts near the sternal angle, across the second costal cartilage.
It runs down the front of the limb.
The posterior upper limb axial line ends at the wrist

The posterior axial line of the upper limb ends at the deltoid insertion, not the wrist.
The anterior line runs almost to the wrist.
The root of the penis is S2

The root of the penis is L1; the rest of the penis and the scrotum are S2/3.
An axial line crosses the scrotum.
C1 has no skin supply

C1 usually has no cutaneous branch; C2 supplies the back of the scalp.
So there is no C1 dermatome.
T10 supplies the umbilicus

T10 supplies the umbilicus; T4 the nipple and T8 the costal margin.
Common sensory level landmarks.
C7 supplies the little finger

C7 supplies the middle finger; C8 the ring and little fingers.
C6 supplies the thumb.
T1 supplies the axilla

T1 supplies the medial side of the elbow region, not the axilla. T2 supplies the axilla.
A Last's detail.
L4 supplies the medial malleolus

L4 supplies the medial leg and malleolus; L5 the dorsum of the foot and great toe; S1 the lateral foot.
A useful map.
S3 supplies the sitting area of the buttock

S3 supplies the sitting area of the buttock and the posterior scrotum or labium.
Saddle anaesthesia involves S3 to S5.
L5 supplies the lateral malleolus

S1 supplies the lateral malleolus, not L5.
L5 is the dorsum and great toe.
S4 supplies the posterior thigh

S4 supplies the perianal skin, not the posterior thigh.
S2 supplies the posterior thigh.
Biceps jerk is C6

Last's gives the biceps jerk as C6 (others say C5/6); triceps C7, knee L3, ankle S1.
Last's assigns single segments.
Knee jerk is L3

The knee jerk is mediated mainly by L3 (with L4) through the femoral nerve.
Reduced in L3/4 root lesions.
Ankle jerk is L5

The ankle jerk is S1, not L5.
L5 has no reliable reflex.
Abductor pollicis brevis is C6

Abductor pollicis brevis is T1, not C6.
It is the classic test of the T1 myotome.
Hip adduction is L2/3

Hip flexion, adduction and medial rotation are L2/3; extension, abduction and lateral rotation are L4/5.
Opposing actions in sequence.
Tibialis posterior is supplied by L4

Tibialis posterior is supplied by L4, with its inverting partner tibialis anterior.
Segmental supply follows inversion.
Gluteus maximus is L4, 5, S1

Gluteus maximus is L5, S1 and S2, not L4, L5, S1.
The other gluteal muscles are L4, L5, S1.
Hip abduction is L2/3

Hip abduction is L4/5, not L2/3.
L2/3 is flexion and adduction.
The plantar response becomes flexor during the second year

An extensor plantar response is normal under one year; it becomes flexor in the second year.
As corticospinal myelination completes.
The anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes depend mainly on S3

The anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes depend on intact sacral segments, mainly S3.
Their return marks the end of spinal shock.
Abdominal reflexes are exaggerated in upper motor neuron lesions

Abdominal reflexes are absent in upper motor neurone lesions, not exaggerated.
Unlike tendon reflexes.
In Beevor's sign the umbilicus moves downwards

In Beevor's sign the umbilicus moves upward when the patient flexes the neck, because the lower abdominal muscles are weak (lesion around T10).
Upward, not downward.
The superior cervical ganglion represents C1-4

The upper four cervical ganglia fuse into the superior cervical ganglion, which gives grey rami to C1 to C4.
The largest cervical ganglion.
Only T1-L2 give white rami

Only T1 to L2 have lateral horn cells, so only they have white rami; every spinal nerve receives a grey ramus.
White rami carry the outflow.
Grey rami are preganglionic

Grey rami carry postganglionic fibres, not preganglionic.
White rami carry preganglionic fibres.
Limb vessels receive sympathetics by fibres running long distances along the arteries

Limb vessels receive their sympathetic fibres from the adjacent peripheral nerves, not from fibres running long distances along the arteries.
So perivascular sympathectomy is ineffective.
Sacral splanchnic nerves are sympathetic

Sacral splanchnic nerves are sympathetic branches of the sacral trunk to the pelvic plexus.
Easily confused with pelvic splanchnics.
Pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic

Pelvic splanchnic nerves are the S2 to S4 parasympathetic outflow; do not confuse the two.
Last's warns about this.
A proximal root lesion reduces sympathetic function in the limb

Sympathetic fibres join the spinal nerves distal to the roots, so a proximal root lesion does not reduce sympathetic function in the limb; a peripheral nerve lesion does.
Sweating helps localise.
Preganglionic fibres to the suprarenal synapse in the coeliac ganglion

Preganglionic fibres to the suprarenal medulla pass through the coeliac ganglion without synapse.
The medullary cells are the postganglionic neurons.
The embryo becomes a fetus after 8 weeks

The developing human is called an embryo for the first eight weeks and a fetus thereafter.
Organogenesis is mostly complete by then.
Neural crest gives Schwann cells

Neural crest gives Schwann cells, as well as the dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia and suprarenal medulla.
A very versatile tissue.
Paraxial mesoderm gives the limb buds

The lateral plate mesoderm gives the limb buds, not the paraxial mesoderm.
Limb muscles migrate in from somites.
Intermediate mesoderm is unsegmented

The lateral plate is the unsegmented mesoderm; intermediate mesoderm shows some segmentation (nephrotomes).
Paraxial mesoderm forms segmented somites.
The stapedial artery is a second arch remnant

The second arch artery disappears except for the stapedial artery.
Which itself does not persist after birth.
Stylopharyngeus is the third arch muscle

Stylopharyngeus is the only muscle of the third arch, supplied by IX.
A favourite fact.
The mandible ossifies in Meckel's cartilage

The mandible ossifies in membrane around Meckel's cartilage, not in the cartilage; Meckel's remnants include the lingula.
Only a small part near the symphysis may involve cartilage.
The 4th arch forms the pulmonary arteries

The sixth arch arteries form the pulmonary arteries (and the ductus on the left), not the fourth.
The fourth forms the aortic arch and right subclavian.
The third pouch forms the inferior parathyroid

The third pouch forms the inferior parathyroid and the thymus.
The parathyroid is pulled down with the thymus.
The fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroid

The dorsal part of the fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroid.
It stays near the upper thyroid.
The second pouch forms the thymus

The second pouch forms the tonsillar crypts (and supratonsillar fossa), not the thymus.
The thymus is third pouch.
The fifth pouch forms the follicular thyroid cells

The fifth pouch forms the ultimobranchial body, which gives the parafollicular (C) cells, not the follicular cells.
Follicular cells come from the thyroid diverticulum.
A branchial fistula tracks between internal and external carotids

A branchial fistula runs from the tonsillar fossa between the internal and external carotids to the skin at the lower anterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
It follows the second cleft and pouch.
An aberrant right subclavian makes the right laryngeal nerve non-recurrent

An aberrant right subclavian artery (1 to 2 percent) makes the right laryngeal nerve non-recurrent.
A thyroid surgery hazard.
The fistula opens at the posterior border of SCM

A branchial fistula opens at the lower anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, not the posterior border.
The anterior border is the typical site.
The chorda tympani is a post-trematic nerve

Last's describes the chorda tympani as a pretrematic nerve (running in front of the first cleft), not post-trematic.
A morphological point.
The anterior fontanelle closes at about 18 months

The anterior fontanelle, between the frontal and parietal bones, closes at about 18 months.
It can be used to assess hydration and intracranial pressure.
The posterior fontanelle closes by the end of the first year

The posterior fontanelle, at the lambda, closes by the end of the first year.
Earlier than the anterior.
The mastoid is aerated at birth

The mastoid is aerated from the beginning of the second year, not at birth.
The antrum is present at birth.
The geniculate ganglion is separated from middle fossa dura at birth

Last's says at birth the tegmen is incomplete, so the geniculate ganglion is in contact with the middle fossa dura.
It is not separated from it.
The squamous and tympanic parts ossify in membrane

The squamous and tympanic parts of the temporal bone ossify in membrane; the petromastoid and styloid parts ossify in cartilage.
A mixed bone.
The foramen of Huschke is temporary

Growing flanges of the tympanic plate enclose a temporary gap, the foramen of Huschke, which normally closes in childhood.
If it persists it can transmit infection.
The facial nerve at birth is protected by the mastoid process

At birth the facial nerve is unprotected, covered only by sternocleidomastoid, because there is no mastoid process.
Care with postauricular incisions in infants.
The spinal cord ends at L1 at birth

At birth the spinal cord ends at L3, not L1.
It reaches L1/2 in adulthood.
